Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Calendar booking API

This API manages calendar bookings for your application. You can create appointments, reserve time slots, check availability, update existing bookings, and cancel reservations through a set of HTTP endpoints.

The API uses standard REST conventions. All requests and responses use JSON. Authentication relies on bearer tokens passed in the Authorization header.

Calendar data is stored with timezone awareness. When you create or retrieve bookings, times reflect the timezone you specify. This prevents confusion across regions and ensures notifications trigger at the correct local time.

Common workflows include checking what time slots exist on a given day, reserving one for a customer, sending them a confirmation, and later updating or canceling the booking if plans change. The API handles conflicts automatically—if someone else books the same slot in the same moment, one request succeeds and the other returns an error with the reason.

Most endpoints return the full booking object with timestamps, participant details, and any attached metadata. Error responses include a code and message you can parse to decide what to show the user.

To get started, authenticate with your API key, then read the endpoints section for specific syntax. The examples folder contains requests for the most common operations.

This API manages calendar bookings for your application. You can create appointments, reserve time slots, check availability, update existing bookings, and cancel reservations through a set of HTTP endpoints.

The API uses standard REST conventions. All requests and responses use JSON. Calendar data is stored with timezone awareness, so when you create or retrieve bookings, times reflect the timezone you specify. This prevents confusion across regions and ensures notifications trigger at the correct local time.

Common workflows include checking available time slots on a given day, reserving one for a customer, and later updating or canceling if plans change. The API handles conflicts automatically—if two people book the same slot simultaneously, one request succeeds and the other returns an error with the reason.

Most endpoints return the full booking object with timestamps, participant details, and any attached metadata. Error responses include a code and message you can parse to decide what to show the user.

To get started, authenticate with your API key, then read the endpoints section for specific syntax. The examples folder contains requests for the most common operations.

**Authentication**

Authenticate all requests using a bearer token in the Authorization header. Include your API key as `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY`. You can generate or rotate API keys from your account settings. Each key remains valid until you revoke it or create a new one. Requests without a valid token receive a 401 Unauthorized response.
